lessons.title: Environmental Impact
lessons.body:
Turkey farming affects the environment mainly through manure, feed, water use, and energy. A single turkey produces about 0.5 kg of manure per day. For a flock of 100 turkeys, that's 50 kg of manure dailyâenough to pollute a small stream if not managed. In Africa, where many farms are near rivers or wells, this is a serious risk. The biggest concerns are nutrient runoff (nitrogen and phosphorus) causing algal blooms in water, greenhouse gas emissions (methane and nitrous oxide from manure), and ammonia from urine and droppings, which can harm air quality and soil.

To reduce impact, start by keeping turkeys away from water sources. Use a buffer zone of at least 30 meters between the flock and any stream, pond, or well. Collect manure daily and store it in a covered pit or pile on concreteânot on bare ground. Covering manure reduces ammonia loss by up to 50% and prevents rain from washing nutrients away. Also, plant trees or shrubs around the farm as windbreaks; they capture dust and ammonia.

Feed efficiency matters. Turkeys convert feed to meat at about 2.5 to 3 kg feed per kg gain. If you waste feed, you waste money and increase environmental load. Use feeders that prevent spillage and store feed in airtight containers to avoid rodents. Buying local feed ingredientsâlike maize, soy, and fishmeal from nearbyâcuts transport emissions. In many African countries, you can mix your own feed using a hammer mill and a scale, reducing cost and carbon footprint.

Energy use on the farm also counts. Incandescent bulbs for brooding use 60-100 watts each; switching to LED (9-15 watts) cuts electricity by 80%. If you use a generator, maintain it well to reduce diesel smoke. Solar panels are increasingly affordable in Africa and can power lights and small pumps. Finally, consider planting a few acres of legume trees like Leucaena or Gliricidiaâthey fix nitrogen, provide shade, and their leaves can be fed to turkeys as a protein supplement, closing nutrient loops.

By managing manure, feed, water, and energy carefully, you can raise turkeys with minimal harm to the environment while saving money. Small changes add up: a 100-bird farm can reduce its nitrogen runoff by half with simple covers and buffers.

lessons.title: Manure Management
lessons.body:
Turkey manure is a valuable resource, not waste. It contains about 1.5% nitrogen, 1% phosphorus, and 0.8% potassiumâsimilar to commercial fertilizers. A 100-bird flock produces roughly 50 kg of fresh manure daily, which over a year is 18 tonnes. If you simply dump it, you lose nutrients and pollute. Proper management turns it into free fertilizer for crops or extra income.

First, collect manure daily. Use a shovel and wheelbarrow, or install slatted floors so droppings fall into a pit below. For deep litter systems, add wood shavings or rice hulls every few days; the litter absorbs moisture and reduces smell. Keep the litter dryâmoisture above 30% encourages flies and ammonia. Aim for 10-15 cm of fresh litter on top. Remove wet spots immediately.

Second, compost the manure before using it. Fresh manure can burn plants and carry pathogens. Composting heats it to 55-65Â°C, killing weed seeds and bacteria. Build a pile 1.5 m high and 2 m wide. Mix manure with carbon materials like straw, maize stalks, or dry leaves in a 1:2 ratio (one part manure to two parts carbon). Turn the pile every 3 days for the first two weeks, then weekly. Keep it as moist as a wrung-out sponge. After 6-8 weeks, it's dark, crumbly, and smells earthy. You can also use a worm binâred wigglers eat manure and produce vermicompost in 4-6 weeks.

Third, store manure safely. If you can't compost immediately, keep it in a covered concrete pit or on a plastic sheet with a tarp on top. This prevents rain from leaching nutrients and stops flies. Never store manure uphill from a well or stream. A simple roof over the pile works.

Fourth, use the compost. Apply 2-4 tonnes per hectare for maize, vegetables, or pasture. It improves soil structure and water retention. You can also sell compost in 50 kg bags to neighboursâa bag can fetch $5-10 in many African markets. For turkey health, keep manure away from feed and water. Wear gloves and boots when handling, and wash hands afterwards. If you notice a bad smell, add more carbon or turn the pile. With good management, manure becomes a profit centre, not a problem.

lessons.title: Energy Efficiency
lessons.body:
Energy is a major cost in turkey farming, especially for brooding and lighting. In Africa, where electricity can be unreliable or expensive, saving energy boosts profits. A typical brooder uses 250 watts for 100 chicks; running it 24/7 for 4 weeks uses about 168 kWhâenough to cost $20-40 depending on local rates. You can cut that by half with simple changes.

Start with insulation. Brooders lose heat through gaps. Use cardboard, old blankets, or straw bales to line the brooder walls and ceiling. A well-insulated brooder can maintain 35Â°C with a 100-watt bulb instead of 250 watts. Also, use a brooder guardâa circle of cardboard or metalâto keep chicks near the heat. This reduces the area you need to heat by 60%. For 100 chicks, a 1.5 m diameter guard is enough.

Switch to LED bulbs. A 9-watt LED gives the same light as a 60-watt incandescent. For a 100-bird grow-out house, you need about 20 lux (bright enough to read a newspaper). That's one 9-watt LED per 10 square meters. Use a timer to turn lights off for 8 hours at night after the first weekâturkeys need darkness to rest. This saves 30% of lighting energy. If you have no grid, solar panels are a good option. A 100-watt panel with a battery can power 10 LED bulbs and a small brooder for a day. Cost: $150-200, payback in 6-12 months.

For heating, consider a rocket stove or biogas. A rocket stove uses twigs and burns hot with little smoke; you can pipe heat into the brooder. Biogas from manure can run a gas brooderâa 2 cubic meter digester produces enough gas for 50 chicks. In many African countries, NGOs or government programs subsidize biogas units. Also, use the sun: a solar wall (black-painted metal or mud) on the south side of the brooder absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night.

Finally, maintain equipment. Clean bulbs and reflectors monthlyâdust cuts light by 20%. Fix leaks in water heaters. If you use a generator, service it every 100 hours and use the correct oil. By combining insulation, LED, timers, and solar, you can cut energy costs by 50-70%. That's money in your pocket and less strain on the grid.

lessons.title: Water Conservation
lessons.body:
Turkeys drink a lot: about 0.5 litres per bird per day for adults, and 0.1 litres for chicks. A 100-bird flock uses 50 litres dailyâ18,000 litres per year. In dry African regions, water is precious. Wasting it costs money and can drain wells. With simple tools, you can cut water use by 30-50%.

First, use nipple drinkers instead of open troughs. Nipple drinkers deliver water on demand and spill almost nothing. Open troughs lose up to 40% to evaporation and splashing. A nipple system for 100 birds costs about $50-80 and pays back in 3-6 months from water savings and drier litter. Install them at the right heightânipples at eye level for chicks, and raise as they grow. Check for leaks daily; a dripping nipple wastes 10 litres a day.

Second, harvest rainwater. In most of Africa, a 20-square-meter roof can collect 1,000 litres from just 50 mm of rain. Install gutters and a 2,000-litre tank (plastic or concrete). Use a first-flush diverter to throw away the first 20 litres of dirty roof water. Filter the rest through cloth into the tank. Cover the tank to prevent evaporation and mosquitoes. You can also dig a small pond lined with clay or plastic to catch runoffâbut fence it to keep turkeys out, as they will foul it.

Third, recycle water. Water used to wash feeders and drinkers can be reused for flushing or for watering trees, not for drinking. Set up a simple greywater system: a bucket under the drinker line catches spills, and you pour it on a garden. Never let wastewater flow into a stream. Also, check your water sourceâif you use a well, install a hand pump or solar pump instead of a diesel pump. A solar pump costs $300-500 but has no fuel cost.

Fourth, manage litter moisture. Wet litter means you're wasting water and creating disease. Fix leaks immediately. If litter is damp, add dry shavings and increase ventilation. Aim for 20-30% moistureâif you squeeze a handful, it should hold together but not drip. Use a cheap moisture meter ($10) or the squeeze test. By combining nipple drinkers, rainwater harvesting, and careful monitoring, you can keep your turkeys healthy with far less water.

lessons.title: Pasture-Based Systems
lessons.body:
Pasture-based turkey farming lets birds roam on grass, eating insects, seeds, and greens. This cuts feed costs by 20-30% and improves meat flavour. It also reduces labour for cleaning and spreads manure naturally. In Africa, this system works well where land is available and climate is mildâavoid very hot or wet seasons. You need a secure fence, a movable shelter, and a plan.

Start with a portable electric net fence. It costs $100-150 for 50 meters and keeps turkeys in and predators out. For 50 birds, a 50x50 meter paddock is enough. Rotate the flock every 2-3 weeks to fresh grass to prevent parasite build-up and let grass recover. A simple rotation: divide land into 4 paddocks and move the shelter and fence each time. Turkeys will eat grass down, so give each paddock 3-4 weeks rest.

Provide a movable shelterâan A-frame or hoop house on skids. It should have a roost (2.5 cm diameter poles) and a covered area for feed and water. Move it with the fence. In rainy season, raise the shelter on a mound or pallets to keep birds dry. You can also use a simple tarp over a frame. For night safety, close the shelter doorâpredators like foxes, snakes, and hawks are common in Africa. A livestock guardian dog or donkey can help.

Feed supplement is still needed. Pasture provides maybe 20% of diet. Give a balanced ration of maize, soy, and minerals in the morning and evening. Use feeders that hang from the shelter to avoid rain. Provide grit (crushed granite) for digestion. Watch for parasitesâturkeys on pasture get worms. Rotate and use a dewormer every 3 months (e.g., fenbendazole). Also, keep water clean and shaded.

Benefits: lower feed bills, healthier birds, and better soil. Turkey droppings fertilize grass, and their scratching breaks up manure. You can also run turkeys behind cattleâthey eat fly larvae and spread manure. In a 1-hectare pasture, you can raise 100-150 turkeys per year with rotation. Start small: 20 birds on 0.2 hectares. Build a mobile pen from bamboo and chicken wire. As you learn, expand. Pasture-based systems are low-cost and sustainable, but require daily attention to fencing, water, and predators.

lessons.title: Organic Turkey Production
lessons.body:
Organic turkey production means no synthetic pesticides, fertilizers, or drugs. You rely on natural feed, preventive health, and humane management. In Africa, this is feasible and can fetch premium pricesâorganic turkey can sell for 30-50% more in cities. But you must follow rules: no antibiotics, no GMO feed, and access to outdoors.

Feed must be 100% organic. That means maize, soy, and wheat grown without chemicals. You can grow your own or buy from certified organic farmers. In many African countries, organic certification is available through groups like Ecocert or local agencies. A typical organic ration: 60% maize, 25% soy, 10% fishmeal (from sustainable sources), 5% minerals and seaweed. Mix with a hammer mill. You can also ferment feedâmix with water and let it sit 2-3 days. Fermentation increases beneficial bacteria, improves digestion, and reduces feed cost by 10%. Add 5% charcoal to prevent toxins.

Health care is preventive. Use herbal remedies: garlic and ginger for respiratory issues, aloe vera for wounds, and neem leaves for external parasites. Keep litter dry and clean. Vaccinate against Newcastle disease and fowl poxâthese are allowed in organic systems. Never use antibiotics; if a bird gets sick, isolate and treat with herbs, or cull if necessary. Use diatomaceous earth in dust baths to control mites. Provide plenty of space: at least 2 square meters per bird outdoors. Rotate pasture to break parasite cycles. Record everythingâfeed, treatments, and movementsâfor certification.

Housing should allow fresh air and sunlight. A simple open-sided shelter with a solid roof works. Perches and nest boxes made from local wood. No synthetic paints or treated timber. Use natural bedding like straw or wood shavings from untreated wood. Water must be cleanârainwater or well water tested for contaminants.

Marketing: label your turkeys as organic and tell your story. Sell directly to restaurants, hotels, or health-conscious consumers. In Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa, organic turkey demand is growing. You can also process on-farm and sell frozen. Start with 20-50 birds to learn. Keep costs low by using family labour and local materials. Organic production is more work but rewards are higher and the system is sustainable for the land and your health.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sustainable Turkey Farming in Africa

Sustainability is not a moral add-on for African turkey producers; it is a margin strategy. Feed is 65â75% of turkey production cost, energy is the second-largest overhead, and manure is either a costly disposal problem or a free input. This Practical Reference module consolidates the six lessons in this unit into field-ready numbers, benchmarks and decision rules for small and medium-scale commercial turkey operations in Africa. Use it as a working document â print it, pin it in the brooder house, and revisit it each cycle.

1. Environmental Impact â What the Numbers Actually Mean

Poultry production contributes an estimated 8% of global livestock greenhouse gas emissions, and within that turkey is a comparatively efficient converter compared with ruminants. The practical sustainability question for an African producer is not global carbon â it is local: odour, flies, ammonia, dust, nitrate leaching into wells, and deforestation for litter material. Manage those five and you have managed the environmental impact of your farm.

Table 1: Environmental footprint benchmarks for turkey production (per bird, per cycle)
IndicatorTypical rangeBest-practice targetManagement lever
Fresh manure output25â40 kg28 kgLitter type, feed conversion
Nitrogen in manure0.5â0.9 kg N0.6 kg NDietary protein, phase feeding
Ammonia emission0.10â0.25 kg NHâ<0.12 kgLitter moisture <25%, ventilation
Water use (drinking + cleaning)25â45 L30 LNipple drinkers, leak repair
Energy use (electric + gas)1.5â3.5 kWh equivalent2.0 kWhInsulation, brooders, solar
Land for feed6â10 mÂ²7 mÂ²Yield, local sourcing, FCR
Sources: FAO, Poultry Development Review (2013); FAO, Livestock's Long Shadow (2006); IPCC, 2006 Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, Vol. 4, Ch. 10.

2. Manure Management â Turn Waste into a Second Product

On a 500-bird cycle you produce roughly 14 tonnes of litter. Sold raw, that is a nuisance. Composted or dried, it is worth USD 60â150 per tonne in most African markets as a soil amendment for horticulture, maize or pasture. The rule is simple: never apply fresh poultry litter directly to crops â it burns roots, spreads pathogens and loses nitrogen. Compost for 6â8 weeks, turning weekly, until internal temperature has passed 55 Â°C for three consecutive days.

Composting and storage decision rules

  • Carbon:nitrogen ratio: target 25â30:1. Turkey litter alone is ~10:1, so blend with maize stover, sawdust, coffee husk or rice hull.
  • Moisture: 50â60%. Squeeze test â a drop or two, not a stream.
  • Cover: roof or tarpaulin. Rain leaches nitrogen and creates runoff into water sources.
  • Distance: store at least 30 m from wells, boreholes and surface water.
  • Biogas option: 1 kg poultry litter yields roughly 0.3â0.5 mÂ³ biogas. A 500-bird farm can offset a meaningful share of cooking or brooder fuel.

3. Energy Efficiency â The Second-Biggest Cost Line

Brooding is the energy peak. In many African operations, the brooder alone accounts for 60â80% of electricity or gas use. Three interventions pay back in under two seasons: (a) insulate the brooder ring with locally available materials (straw bales, sisal, cardboard), (b) step down brooder temperature on schedule rather than by feel, and (c) install a 300â500 W solar panel with battery to run lights and fans, keeping the grid or generator for brooding only.

Table 2: Energy and water efficiency interventions â cost, saving and payback
InterventionIndicative cost (USD)Annual savingPayback
Brooder insulation (straw/sisal)20â6015â25% of brooding fuel<1 cycle
Nipple drinker retrofit (500 birds)120â25030â50% of water use4â8 months
LED lighting40â9060â75% of lighting energy2â4 months
300 W solar + battery350â70040â70% of grid/generator18â30 months
Rainwater harvesting (10 mÂ³ tank)200â50020â40% of water bill12â24 months
Compost shed + cover150â400Manure value uplift + N retention1â2 cycles
Sources: FAO, Poultry Development Review (2013); GIZ, Energy Efficiency in Agriculture (2019); SNV, Solar for Productive Use in Africa (2021). Costs are indicative for East/West Africa, 2023â2024.

4. Water Conservation â Do More with Every Litre

Turkeys drink roughly 1.5â2.0 times their feed intake by weight. A 15 kg finisher drinks 400â600 ml/day. On a 500-bird farm, total cycle water use is 15,000â22,000 litres â a real constraint in dry-season Africa. The biggest losses are not drinking water; they are spillage from open troughs, leaking pipes and over-washing. Nipple or cup drinkers cut consumption by 30â50% and keep litter dry, which in turn cuts ammonia and pododermatitis.

  • Check drinker lines weekly for leaks â a single dripping nipple wastes 30â60 L/day.
  • Reuse final-rinse water for floor washing or compost moisture, not for drinking.
  • Harvest roof runoff: a 100 mÂ² roof in a 700 mm rainfall zone yields ~70,000 L/year.
  • Never use untreated surface water for drinking â assume contamination.
â  SAFETY WARNING â MANURE, AMMONIA AND GAS HAZARDS

Confined poultry houses and covered manure pits can accumulate ammonia, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide to lethal concentrations. Never enter a pit or a closed house to clean or inspect without forced ventilation for at least 30 minutes and a second person standing by. Ammonia above 25 ppm irritates eyes and lungs and predisposes birds to respiratory disease. Always wear a dust mask and gloves when handling litter, and wash hands and boots before moving between houses to prevent disease spread. Store manure away from wells, boreholes and dwellings â at least 30 m â and never burn litter indoors.

5. Pasture-Based and Organic Systems â Premium Markets

Free-range and organic turkey production in Africa commands 20â60% price premiums in urban and export-adjacent markets (Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Cape Town). The trade-offs are real: slower growth (20â24 weeks to market vs 16â20), higher feed conversion (3.0â3.8 vs 2.4â2.8) and heavier predation losses. The economics only work if you have secure premium buyers and access to good pasture. Key requirements:

  • Pasture: rotate paddocks every 7â10 days; stock at 150â250 birds/ha; include legumes (lucerne, desmodium) to cut protein cost.
  • Shelter: mobile houses or shade trees â turkeys are poor heat regulators and need 2â3 mÂ² shade per 10 birds in hot climates.
  • Organic certification: requires certified organic feed, no synthetic drugs or GMO, and a 12-month conversion period. Certification bodies active in Africa include Ecocert, Ceres and Control Union.
  • Predator control: electric netting, guardian dogs, night housing â budget 3â8% mortality against 2â4% indoors.

6. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Litter moisture: measure weekly â keep below 25% to control ammonia and flies.
  2. Feed conversion: record FCR per pen per cycle; target 2.4â2.8 for confined, 3.0â3.8 for free-range.
  3. Water: check drinkers for leaks every Monday; log daily consumption per 100 birds.
  4. Manure: compost 6â8 weeks, turn weekly, cover with roof or tarp, store >30 m from water.
  5. Energy: step down brooder temperature on schedule; insulate; consider solar for lights and fans.
  6. Mortality: investigate any pen exceeding 3% per week â usually ventilation, water or disease.
  7. Records: one page per cycle: feed in, birds out, water, energy, manure sold. No records, no sustainability.
  8. Safety: never enter pits or closed houses without ventilation and a buddy.

Further Reading (free, official)

  • FAO â Poultry Production and Products (technical guidance and country case studies).
  • FAO â Poultry Development Review (2013, PDF) â includes environmental and manure management chapters.
  • FAO â Livestock's Long Shadow (2006) â baseline environmental footprint data for poultry and livestock.
  • IPCC â 2006 Guidelines, Vol. 4, Ch. 10: Emissions from Livestock and Manure Management.
  • GIZ â Energy Efficiency in Agriculture (2019, PDF) â applicable to African farm-scale energy planning.

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Turkey Farming: Sustainable Turkey Farming. Figures are indicative for small and medium commercial operations in sub-Saharan Africa and should be validated against local input prices and market conditions before investment decisions.

quiz.q: How much manure does a single turkey produce per day?
quiz.explanation: A turkey produces about 0.5 kg of manure daily, so 100 turkeys produce 50 kg.

quiz.q: What is the recommended buffer zone between turkeys and a water source?
quiz.explanation: A 30-meter buffer prevents nutrient runoff from reaching streams or wells.

quiz.q: Covering manure reduces ammonia loss by up to what percentage?
quiz.explanation: Covering manure can cut ammonia loss by about 50%, preserving nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is the typical feed conversion ratio for turkeys?
options: B) 2.5-3 kg feed per kg gain
C) 5-6 kg feed per kg gain
D) 10 kg feed per kg gain
quiz.explanation: Turkeys convert feed at about 2.5 to 3 kg feed per kg of body weight gain.

quiz.q: Which lighting change can cut brooder electricity by 80%?
quiz.explanation: LED bulbs use 9-15 watts compared to 60-100 watts for incandescent, saving about 80%.

quiz.q: What percentage of nitrogen does turkey manure typically contain?
quiz.explanation: Turkey manure contains about 1.5% nitrogen, 1% phosphorus, and 0.8% potassium.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture level for turkey litter?
quiz.explanation: Litter moisture of 20-30% is ideal; higher moisture encourages flies and ammonia.

quiz.q: During composting, what temperature range kills pathogens and weed seeds?
quiz.explanation: Composting at 55-65Â°C for several days kills most pathogens and weed seeds.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio of manure to carbon material for composting?
quiz.explanation: A 1:2 ratio of manure to carbon (e.g., straw) provides good aeration and carbon-nitrogen balance.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile in the first two weeks?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 3 days for the first two weeks speeds up decomposition and heats the pile.

quiz.q: What wattage LED bulb can replace a 60-watt incandescent for lighting?
quiz.explanation: A 9-watt LED provides similar light output to a 60-watt incandescent.

quiz.q: How many hours of darkness per night are recommended for growing turkeys after the first week?
quiz.explanation: 8 hours of darkness allows turkeys to rest and saves lighting energy.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a 100-watt solar panel with battery for a small farm?
quiz.explanation: A 100-watt solar panel with battery costs about $150-200 and can pay back in 6-12 months.

quiz.q: Which heating method uses twigs and burns hot with little smoke?
quiz.explanation: A rocket stove uses twigs and provides efficient, low-smoke heat for brooders.

quiz.q: How much water does an adult turkey drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Adult turkeys drink about 0.5 litres per day; chicks need about 0.1 litres.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of nipple drinkers over open troughs?
options: B) Reduce water waste by up to 40%
quiz.explanation: Nipple drinkers deliver water on demand and reduce spillage and evaporation by up to 40%.

quiz.q: How much rainwater can a 20-square-meter roof collect from 50 mm of rain?
quiz.explanation: 20 mÂ² Ã 0.05 m = 1 mÂ³ = 1,000 litres.

quiz.q: What is a first-flush diverter used for?
options: B) To discard the first dirty rainwater
quiz.explanation: A first-flush diverter throws away the first 20 litres of roof water, which contain dirt and bird droppings.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stocking density for pasture-based turkeys?
options: B) 100-150 birds per hectare per year
quiz.explanation: With rotation, 1 hectare can support 100-150 turkeys per year.

quiz.q: How often should you rotate pasture paddocks for turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Rotating every 2-3 weeks prevents parasite build-up and allows grass to recover.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a brooder guard?
options: B) To keep chicks near heat and reduce heated area
quiz.explanation: A brooder guard confines chicks near the heat source, reducing the area to heat by up to 60%.

quiz.q: What percentage of a pasture-based turkey's diet can come from pasture?
quiz.explanation: Pasture can provide about 20% of a turkey's diet; the rest must be supplemented.

quiz.q: What is a good natural dewormer for pasture-raised turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Fenbendazole is an effective dewormer; use every 3 months in pasture systems.

quiz.q: In organic turkey production, what is the maximum percentage of feed that can be non-organic?
quiz.explanation: Organic certification requires 100% organic feed; no synthetic pesticides or GMOs.

quiz.q: Which herb is commonly used as a natural remedy for respiratory issues in turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Garlic and ginger have antimicrobial properties and can help with respiratory infections.

quiz.q: What is the minimum outdoor space per bird in organic turkey production?
quiz.explanation: Organic standards typically require at least 2 square meters per bird outdoors.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of fermenting feed for turkeys?
options: B) Improves digestion and reduces cost
quiz.explanation: Fermentation increases beneficial bacteria, improves digestion, and can reduce feed cost by 10%.

quiz.q: What is diatomaceous earth used for in organic turkey production?
options: B) To control external parasites like mites
quiz.explanation: Diatomaceous earth in dust baths helps control mites and lice naturally.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is allowed in organic turkey production?
quiz.explanation: Vaccines for Newcastle disease and fowl pox are allowed; antibiotics and hormones are not.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to test litter moisture without a meter?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing a handful: if it holds together but doesn't drip, moisture is about 20-30%.
